logo-link.what: A logo that links to the home page. It tells people whose site they are on and gives them a quick way back to the start.
uses: Header or top bar of a website or app.
Footer, so people can return home after reading to the end.
Sign-in pages and emails that carry the brand.
avoid: Placing it next to a separate Home link that goes to the same page; keep just one.
Using the logo as the only way to reach important sections; add real navigation.
practices: Put it in the top left, where people look for it.
Give the link a name that includes the brand name.
Give the image useful alt text or use the name as text.
Link to the home page, and skip the link when already on it.

collapse-toggle.what: A button that folds a panel or sidebar away and brings it back. It gives people more room for content without removing the panel.
uses: Collapsing a sidebar menu down to icons.
Hiding a side panel on small screens.
Giving more width to a table or editor.
avoid: Hiding content people need to finish a task; keep it visible instead.
Showing or hiding a short block of text; use an accordion or disclosure.
practices: Say what the button will do, and update the label when the state changes.
Tell assistive technology whether the region is open with the expanded state.
Remember the choice for the next visit.
Keep the button in the same spot in both states.

skip-navigation.what: A link at the very top of a page that jumps straight to the main content. Keyboard and screen reader users use it to avoid tabbing through the menu on every page.
uses: Pages with a long header or menu before the content.
Any site that people navigate by keyboard.
Sites that must meet accessibility standards.
avoid: Replacing good page structure; headings and landmarks are still needed.
Hiding it permanently; it must appear when it receives focus.
practices: Make it the first thing keyboard focus reaches.
Show it clearly when focused.
Point it to a target that can take focus.
Use words like 'Skip to main content'.
Use one main area per page.

link-column.what: A short heading with a list of related links beneath it. Several columns side by side organise many links by topic.
uses: Website footers with product, company and help links.
Site maps.
Related links at the end of an article or help page.
avoid: Main navigation people use all the time; use a navigation bar or menu.
Long lists of links in one column; split by topic or search instead.
practices: Give each column a clear topic title.
Keep columns to about eight links or fewer.
Write link text that names the destination.
Order links by how often people need them.

page-heading.what: The block at the top of a page that gives its title, often with a short description and status details. It tells people where they are and what the page is for.
uses: Top of an application page or settings page.
Top of a documentation page.
Record pages that show a status next to the title.
avoid: Long introductions; put those in the page body.
Repeating the site name as the title; name the page itself.
practices: Use exactly one main heading per page.
Keep the title short and specific.
Add one sentence of subtitle at most.
Show status with a word as well as a colour.
Place it in the same spot on every page.

section-heading.what: A title that introduces a section of a page, sometimes with a short intro. It helps people scan and decide whether to read the section.
uses: Dividing a long form into groups.
Settings pages with several topics.
Documentation and articles with several parts.
avoid: Labelling a single control; use a form label instead.
Styling plain text bigger; use headings only to introduce real sections.
practices: Keep heading levels in order without skipping.
Make the title say what the section is about.
Keep any intro to one or two sentences.
Use the same style for every section on a page.

feature-item.what: A small block that presents one feature with an icon, a short title and a sentence. Several together give a quick overview of what something offers.
uses: Feature lists on a product or marketing page.
Showing first steps on an empty dashboard.
Summarising benefits on a landing page.
avoid: Content that needs long explanation; write a full section or article.
Steps that must be done in order; use a numbered list.
practices: Write the title as a benefit in a few words.
Keep the description to one sentence.
Use icons that fit the meaning, and treat them as decoration.
Use the same layout for every item in a group.

captioned-media.what: An image or video shown in a fixed frame, with a caption explaining it. The fixed shape stops the page from jumping while the media loads.
uses: Photos in articles and posts.
Gallery images with a source and time.
Screenshots that need an explanation.
avoid: Purely decorative pictures; skip the caption.
Long explanations; put them in the body text next to the image.
practices: Reserve the frame size before the media loads.
Write alt text that says what matters in the image.
Keep captions short and place them consistently.
Make caption text readable on any image.
Add source and date when they help.

thumbnail-strip.what: A row of small preview images that people click to choose which large image to see. It shows what is available at a glance.
uses: Product or photo galleries.
Choosing a frame or version of a video.
Media pickers with a limited number of items.
avoid: Very large sets of images; use a grid with paging or search.
Images that look the same at a small size; use text labels.
practices: Mark the current thumbnail with more than a colour change.
Give each thumbnail a name for screen readers.
Keep thumbnails the same size and shape.
Let people use arrow keys and tabbing to move through them.

video-player.what: A player that shows a video with play, pause, volume and a progress bar. It can also flag a live or recorded feed.
uses: Tutorials and product demos.
Live streams.
Recordings people review, such as meetings or camera footage.
avoid: Very short, silent loops; use an animated image or short silent video.
Content that is mostly text; write it out instead.
practices: Show controls and keep them keyboard accessible.
Never start playing with sound automatically.
Provide captions for speech.
Show a poster image and load the video only when needed.
Say clearly when a stream is live.

call-to-action.what: The button or link that asks people to take the next step, such as signing up. A section usually has one main action and sometimes a quieter second choice.
uses: Hero sections and page headers.
Empty pages that need a first step.
Emails with one clear task.
avoid: Giving several equal options; pick one main action and make the rest quieter.
Navigation to other pages; use regular links.
practices: Use one main action per section.
Start the label with a verb that says what happens.
Make the main action look stronger than the alternative.
Keep the button large enough to tap easily.

fine-print.what: Small text for legal notes, copyright, version numbers and policy links. It has to be available but should not compete with the main content.
uses: Page footers.
Email footers.
Sign-in and sign-up pages with terms and privacy links.
avoid: Important conditions people must know before acting; place them next to the action in normal text.
Hiding key information in tiny text.
practices: Keep it readable with enough contrast and size.
Keep it on a single line where possible.
Link to full policies rather than copying them.
Place it in the same spot on every page.

big-number.what: One large figure with a short sentence and its source. It makes a single fact stand out.
uses: Highlighting a key statistic in an article.
Showing a live count next to a video or chart.
Summarising a headline result in a report.
avoid: Comparing several numbers; use a row of stat cards or a table.
Numbers without context; add what they measure.
practices: Say what the number measures right beside it.
Name the source and date.
Write the sign, thousands separators and unit.
Use it for only one or two key facts per page.

summary-tile.what: A small tile showing a count and a status, such as '3 offline'. Clicking it filters the list below to those items.
uses: Overview of how many records have each status.
Quick filters above a table or list.
Dashboards that show what needs attention.
avoid: Showing trends over time; use a chart.
Counts that do nothing when clicked, if there are many; use plain stat cards.
practices: Pair status colour with a word.
Show which filter is active.
Keep counts up to date after changes.
Make tiles large enough to click or tap easily.

heat-row.what: One row of a heat map, with a label and coloured cells where shade shows size. It lets people compare values along a line.
uses: Busy hours by weekday.
Availability or capacity grids.
Activity over time per resource.
avoid: Reading exact values only; use a table.
Showing trends in a single series; use a line chart.
practices: Print the value in each cell as well as the shade.
Label every row and column.
Use a single colour scale from light to dark.
Keep the shade steps easy to tell apart.

column-header.what: The title of a column in a board of cards, with a count of items and sometimes a limit. It shows where work is piling up.
uses: Kanban boards with stages like To do and Done.
Grouped lists with a count per group.
Boards that limit work in progress.
avoid: Plain tables; use column headings with sorting instead.
Very many columns; filter or group differently.
practices: Show the number of cards in each column.
Show the limit and flag clearly when it is exceeded.
Keep titles short.
Do not rely on colour alone to show the limit is exceeded.

row-select.what: Checkboxes at the start of table rows, with one at the top to select all. People pick several records and then act on them together.
uses: Bulk delete, archive or export from a table.
Moving or assigning many items at once.
Comparing chosen rows.
avoid: Tables where only a single action per row is needed; use row buttons.
Choosing just one row from a few; use radio buttons.
practices: Name each checkbox after its row for screen readers.
Show how many rows are selected.
Show the available bulk actions as soon as something is selected.
Make select all clear about what it covers, such as this page or all results.

formatting-toolbar.what: A row of small buttons for formatting text, such as bold, italic, lists and links. It sits above a text area that supports rich text.
uses: Writing comments or descriptions with formatting.
Editing articles or emails.
Rich notes fields.
avoid: Plain text fields; leave the toolbar out.
Very long documents needing many options; use a full editor with menus.
practices: Use familiar icons with text names for assistive technology.
Show which formats are on.
Support keyboard shortcuts such as Ctrl+B.
Group related buttons and keep the set small.

applied-filters.what: A row showing which filters are currently active, each as a tag that can be removed. It also gives a way to clear them all and the number of results.
uses: Above search results or lists that have been filtered.
Product listings with several filters.
Empty results, to show what caused them.
avoid: When no filter is active; show nothing.
Choosing filters; use a filter panel or menu for that.
practices: Show every active filter, never hide any.
Let people remove one filter with one click.
Offer Clear all when more than one is active.
Show the result count and update it right away.

card-skeleton.what: A grey outline shaped like a card, shown while the real card is loading. It tells people content is coming and keeps the page from jumping.
uses: Grids and feeds that load content after the page appears.
Product, video or article cards.
Slow data that takes more than a moment.
avoid: Quick loads under about a second; show nothing instead.
Actions in progress such as saving; use a spinner or progress message.
practices: Match the size and shape of the real card.
Replace it in place when content arrives.
Hide the shapes from screen readers and announce loading instead.
Use a calm look and avoid fast flashing.

date-picker.what: A field for choosing a date, usually through the browser's calendar or typing. Shortcuts can speed up the most common choices.
uses: Due dates, start dates and report dates.
Booking or scheduling a single day.
Filtering by a date.
avoid: Birthdates and other dates far in the past; use separate day, month and year fields.
Choosing a period; use a date range picker.
practices: Use the native date input where possible.
Label the field and state the allowed range.
Offer shortcuts like Today and Tomorrow.
Allow typing as well as picking.
Show the date format people should use.

time-picker.what: A field for choosing a time of day. It follows the person's 12 or 24 hour habit and often moves in set steps.
uses: Start times and reminders.
Opening hours.
Scheduling appointments.
avoid: Lengths of time such as 90 minutes; use a duration picker.
Both a date and a time; use a date and time picker.
practices: Use the native time input.
Use steps such as 15 minutes when exact minutes do not matter.
Show the time zone when it could be unclear.
Label the field clearly.

datetime-picker.what: A pair of fields for a date and a time, together describing one moment. Keeping them separate makes each easy to fill in and correct.
uses: When a task starts or access expires.
Scheduling a message or publication.
Setting a deadline with a time.
avoid: Date only; use a date picker.
A start and an end; use a date range picker.
practices: Group the date and time under one label.
Show the time zone.
Store the moment in a standard form such as UTC.
Check that the moment is allowed, for example not in the past.

date-range-picker.what: A control to choose a start and end date. Presets like Last 7 days make common periods quick, and the end stays after the start.
uses: Report periods.
Booking time off or travel dates.
Filtering lists by date.
avoid: A single day; use a date picker.
Ranges of time within one day; use a time range input.
practices: Offer common presets.
Keep the end date on or after the start date.
Show the length of the chosen range.
Label the start and the end clearly.
Say whether the end date is included.

time-range-input.what: Two time fields for a start and an end, usually with the resulting length. It helps people set periods within a day, including overnight ones.
uses: Opening hours.
Work shifts.
Booking windows.
avoid: Periods across several days; use a date range picker.
Only a length of time; use a duration picker.
practices: Show the length that results.
Say clearly when the end is the next day.
Validate on the server as well.
Label start and end clearly.
Use steps that suit the task, such as 15 minutes.

duration-picker.what: A control for entering a length of time, such as hours and minutes. Quick choices cover usual lengths while fields allow exact values.
uses: Meeting lengths.
Timeouts and retention periods.
Reminder offsets.
avoid: A specific time of day; use a time picker.
A start and end; use a time range input.
practices: Show units next to each field.
Offer common lengths as quick buttons.
Accept values like 90 minutes and tidy them up.
Set sensible minimum and maximum limits.

timezone-selector.what: A control for choosing a time zone, often with a button to use the person's own. It prevents mix-ups when schedules cross regions.
uses: Account or site settings.
Scheduling events for people in other places.
Reports that depend on local time.
avoid: Sites where everything uses one fixed zone; just state the zone.
Guessing the zone silently; let people confirm it.
practices: Detect the person's zone and let them change it.
Show the zone's current offset or local time.
Make the list searchable and use readable place names.
Store the zone by its standard name.

month-year-switcher.what: Buttons and selects for moving a calendar or report between months and years. Arrows handle small steps and the selects allow big jumps.
uses: Calendar headers.
Monthly reports.
Browsing archives by month.
avoid: Picking one date to submit; use a date picker.
Browsing only a few days; use simple next and previous links.
practices: Name the previous and next buttons with the month they lead to.
Show the current month and year clearly.
Limit years to a useful range.
Let people return to today quickly.

mini-calendar.what: A small month grid that shows dates in context. Days can be marked as today, selected, holidays or days with events.
uses: Sidebars on calendar pages.
Filtering a list by day.
Showing which days have events.
avoid: Picking a single date in a form; a date input is simpler.
Detailed schedules with times; use a full calendar view.
practices: Mark today and the selected day clearly, with more than colour.
Name each day with its full date for screen readers.
Start the week on the day people expect.
Make day cells large enough to tap.

detail-panel.what: A block that shows everything about a single record: its name, status, actions and properties. It answers what this is and what can be done with it.
uses: Main area of a record's page.
Side panel for a selected table row.
Quick view of a customer, device or order.
avoid: Comparing many records; use a table.
Editing many fields at once; use a form.
practices: Put the name and status first, then actions.
Show properties as aligned label and value pairs.
Keep the main action prominent and others in a menu.
Show only the most useful facts and link to the rest.

parent-child-tabs.what: A page for one record with tabs for the related records it owns, such as a project with tabs for tasks and members. The main record stays visible while people browse its parts.
uses: A customer with orders and contacts.
A site with its devices and users.
A project with tasks and files.
avoid: Unrelated sections; use general navigation.
Only one kind of related item; list it on the page.
practices: Keep the parent's summary visible on every tab.
Show a count on each tab.
Give each tab its own web address.
Name tabs after the kind of child records.

child-list-tab.what: The content of a tab that lists records belonging to a parent. It looks and works like a normal list but is limited to that parent.
uses: Showing a customer's orders.
Listing the people in a team.
Showing items in a folder or project.
avoid: Lists of unrelated records; use a regular list page.
Records that rarely have children; show a short list on the main page.
practices: Use the same tools as other lists, such as search and sorting.
Make Add pre-fill the parent.
Show an empty state with a way to add the first item.
Show the count in the header.

activity-feed.what: A timeline of changes to a record, showing who did what and when. It builds trust and helps explain why something looks different.
uses: History tab on a record.
Audit logs for administrators.
Team updates on a project.
avoid: Notifications that need a reaction; use alerts or an inbox.
Detailed technical logs; use a log viewer.
practices: Group entries by day.
Show who, what and when for each entry.
Show old and new values for edits.
Load older entries with a button rather than endless scrolling.
Write entries as plain sentences.

delete-blocked-notice.what: A message that explains why something cannot be deleted because other records depend on it. It lists the blockers and what to do instead.
uses: Deleting a customer who still has orders.
Removing a category that still contains items.
Deleting an account with active subscriptions.
avoid: Deletes that work; use a normal confirmation.
Errors with no clear cause; explain the actual problem instead.
practices: Say plainly why it cannot be deleted.
Link to each blocking record.
Offer a safe alternative such as archiving.
Show counts so the size of the problem is clear.

confirm-action-panel.what: A full page that asks people to confirm a serious action. It has room to explain what will happen, what is kept and to name the action on the button.
uses: Deleting an account, site or project.
Revoking access for a user.
Stopping a process that affects many people.
avoid: Small, easily undone actions; use undo or a quick dialog.
Routine actions; skip the confirmation to avoid habit clicking.
practices: Say what will be lost and what will be kept.
Name the action on the button, such as Delete site.
Add a Cancel link that goes back.
Ask for an extra check for irreversible actions.
Make the danger button look different.

user-chip.what: A small element in the top corner showing the signed-in person's avatar, name and role. It usually opens an account menu.
uses: Top bars of web applications.
Opening profile, settings and sign out.
Showing which account is active.
avoid: Public pages with no sign-in; show a Sign in button instead.
Long lists of people; use a table row or card.
practices: Place it at the top right.
Show the name or give the button an accessible name.
Include Sign out in the menu.
Let it shrink to just the avatar on small screens.

panel-header.what: The top row of a panel or card with its title, a short description and actions. It says what the panel shows and what can be done with it.
uses: Dashboard panels and cards.
Table and chart frames.
Settings sections in a panel.
avoid: Page titles; use a page heading.
Panels with no title or actions; skip the header.
practices: Keep the title short and about one topic.
Place actions next to the title.
Limit actions to the most useful few.
Let actions wrap on narrow screens.

pin-control.what: A toggle that pins an item so it stays easy to find, for instance at the top of a list or on a dashboard. It shows whether the item is pinned.
uses: Pinning favourites to a dashboard.
Keeping important items at the top of a list.
Saving shortcuts to frequently used pages.
avoid: Marking something as done; use a checkbox.
Saving to a personal collection; use a bookmark or favourite action.
practices: Show the state in words as well as the icon.
Announce the change to screen readers.
Save at once and undo if saving fails.
Name the item being pinned in the label.

theme-toggle.what: A control to switch the look of an interface between themes such as light and dark. It follows the system setting by default and remembers the choice.
uses: Settings and account pages.
Top bar shortcut for switching between light and dark.
Reading in different lighting.
avoid: Basic colour changes with no real need; follow the system setting.
Sites with a single fixed look.
practices: Offer an automatic option that follows the system setting.
Show all choices at once.
Remember the choice for the next visit.
Apply it before the page appears to avoid flashes.

email-fallback.what: An email link paired with the visible address and a Copy button. It covers people whose device has no mail app set up.
uses: Contact and support pages.
Sharing a report by email.
Any link that starts an email.
avoid: Long conversations; use a contact form or a chat tool.
Sensitive details in the link; avoid putting personal data in it.
practices: Show the address in plain text.
Add a Copy button and confirm when copied.
Prefill a clear subject line.
Keep personal data out of the link.
